articles.title: A Vermont farmer turned a 100-acre family dairy into a 550-acre conservation program, protecting soil, water and wildlife across the farm
articles.summary: US News: The Choiniere family farm in northern Vermont has grown from a small dairy started with 14 cows on 100 acres into a much larger operation while placin.
articles.body: The Choiniere family farm in northern Vermont has grown from a small dairy started with 14 cows on 100 acres into a much larger operation while placing greater attention on the land around it. Today, the farm is part of a 550-acre dairy operation where conservation work focuses on soil, water and wildlife. The changes have taken place over several generations, with the family working with the US Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service(NRCS) to address erosion, manage manure and improve the health of the farm’s fields and waterways.The journey of 100-acre Vermont dairy farm began with 14 cowsThe Choiniere family has farmed in northern Vermont for generations. According to NRCS, Guy Choiniere is a fourth-generation Vermont farmer, while the Sand County Foundation reports that the family has been farming the property since 1945.The farm’s early story was much smaller. Guy recalled that the family began with 14 cows on 100 acres. His father, Henry, worked with his siblings, sharing equipment, labour and nutrients to make the farm productive. Over time, that small dairy developed into one of Vermont’s leading dairy farms.The family’s relationship with conservation began more directly around two decades ago, when NRCS technical service providers approached Guy and Henry about problems involving soil and water. Farm cows could reach the Rock River, which damaged the stream banks and allowed soil and manure nutrients to wash into the water.How the family changed its approach towards conservation The Choinieres gradually introduced practices intended to keep nutrients on the farm and reduce the movement of soil and manure into waterways.The Sand County Foundation reports that the family planted 5,000 trees along the banks of the Rock River to help control erosion and improve water quality. A 51-acre river corridor easement was also established, allowing the river to move naturally without being dredged. Along 12,000 feet of riverbank, a permanent 50-foot strip of naturally vegetated land provides another layer of protection.The wider farm includes 242 acres of farmland and 70 acres of woodland, with the Rock River and its tributaries running through the property. The Sand County Foundation reports that these soil-health and erosion-control measures have helped keep the farm productive despite more severe storms, heavier rainfall and periods of drought in north-western Vermont.Transforming the management of manure through compostingOne of the most important changes involved the way the farm handled manure. With help from NRCS, the Choinieres replaced conventional liquid manure storage with a compost bedded pack system. According to NRCS, the system contains a covered area where cows are kept on a solid bed made from materials including hay and sawdust. Manure is collected in the bedding instead of being exposed to rainfall and running off towards nearby water.During winter, the cows are fed hay inside large hoop barns. Excess hay becomes bedding and absorbs manure. According to the Sand County Foundation, pigs are later allowed into the barns when the cows return to rotational grazing in May, helping speed up the composting process before the finished material is spread on fields.The resulting compost provides nutrients for the soil. NRCS reports that the material can produce usable forms of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, along with other nutrients, after being left to compost for roughly six months to a year.Why did the farm move towards organic and grass-fed productionConservation also became connected with the family’s approach to dairy production. The Sand County Foundation reports that Guy began studying organic farming after facing an unstable conventional milk market in the 1990s. He eventually converted the farm to organic production and later changed 25 acres of corn to permanent hay and pasture as the family moved towards a fully grass-fed herd.The decision fitted closely with the conservation work already taking place. According to NRCS, the family found that many organic farming requirements aligned with the conservation practices it was already following. Guy also told NRCS that composting had allowed him to stop using fertiliser for 25 years, while supporting the growth of grass used to feed the cattle.The farm’s organic milk also receives a premium price, according to NRCS, giving the environmental changes a direct connection with the farm’s economic model.Family legacy in conservation passed onto the next generationAs per NRCS, the family plans to continue adding measures such as windbreaks, forest management and wildlife structures, including a bat house.The farm’s conservation story now includes education as well as farming. Guy is an instructor for the Champlain Basin Watershed Initiative, a partnership involving Vermont, New York and Quebec. Through the programme, elementary school teachers learn about watershed issues and how agricultural conservation can affect water quality. For the Choinieres, the conservation plan remains an ongoing process instead of a completed project.The Sand County Foundation reports that Guy’s family has expanded what it produces and sells, including beef, milk, pork, chicken, eggs, honey and baked goods through a farm store.The Choiniere Family Farm received Vermont’s Conservation Farmers of the Year recognition in 2009 and became the first New England recipient from Vermont of the Leopold Conservation Award. Its story shows how growth of a family dairy can happen alongside efforts to protect the resources that make farming possible.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 2 Indian students die in Canada air accident during flight training
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Two Indian students have died in an air accident in Canada while undergoing flight training, the Consulate General of India in Vancouver said in an X .
articles.body: Two Indian students have died in an air accident in Canada while undergoing flight training, the Consulate General of India in Vancouver said in an X post on Sunday.The deceased were identified as Manoj Sivakumar from Tamil nadu and Srisaran Thirugnanasambantham from Puducherry. Canadian search and rescue services and law enforcement authorities have launched an investigation to establish what happened.The incident occurred during a flight-training exercise, although the exact circumstances surrounding the accident remain unclear.Separately, Canadian broadcast media outlet CBC News reported a similar aircraft accident on Saturday, in which a Cessna 172 operated by Harv's Air, a flight school based in St Andrews, Manitoba, crashed near Kisbey, Saskatchewan, killing both people on board.The aircraft was carrying two licensed pilots on a night cross-country flight from Regina to Steinbach, Manitoba. They had planned to stop in Carlyle, Saskatchewan, during the journey, According to the outlet, the pilots had hired the aircraft as part of efforts to accumulate the flight hours needed for commercial pilot licences.Concern was raised after the aircraft did not reach its destination as expected. articles.title: ‘Playing dog whistles’: Raja Krishnamoorthi slams US education dept after Bo French’s South Asian student post
articles.summary: US News: Democratic Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi has criticised the US Department of Education over its “Make college football great again” post, saying it .
articles.body: Democratic Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi has criticised the US Department of Education over its “Make college football great again” post, saying it came days after Republican Texas Railroad Commission candidate Bo French faced backlash for comments about South Asian students at the University of Texas.Krishnamoorthi said the Education Department appeared to be “playing dog whistles” to French’s tune, referring to the controversy that erupted after French posted a photograph of South Asian students cheering for the University of Texas Longhorns. “South Asian Americans are as American as anyone,” Krishnamoorthi said.What did the US Education Department post?The US Department of Education posted a graphic on September 19 showing a packed college football stadium with the words “MAKE COLLEGE FOOTBALL GREAT AGAIN” and “MAKE EDUCATION GREAT AGAIN”.The post drew criticism on social media, with some users connecting its “college football” message to the controversy surrounding French's comments about South Asian students at the University of Texas. Some questioned whether the department's post could be seen as support for or an endorsement of French's remarks. The department's post itself did not mention French or the University of Texas.What did Bo French post about South Asian students?The controversy began after French, the Republican nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, shared a photograph of South Asian students celebrating the University of Texas' football victory.French wrote that he had heard “UT graduation this year looked like this” and added that “the problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined”.In another post featuring the same photograph, French said social media was showing “how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners”. His comments drew bipartisan criticism, including from several Texas Republicans.Republican Senator John Cornyn condemned French's post, asking whether other Republican officials would denounce what he described as intolerance and racism. Texas Republican lawmakers including Lacey Hull and Jared Patterson also criticised the post.French later defended his remarks and argued that the University of Texas' admissions practices disadvantaged Texans, according to the Texas Tribune.The controversy has also drawn attention to the makeup of the University of Texas. Reuters reported that international students account for 4.3 per cent of UT Austin undergraduates, while more than 80 per cent of students are Texas residents.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: He made a work presentation that morning: Family of Bangladeshi-origin AI scientist seeks probe into Irfan Al-Hussaini's July death in Pao Alto, says something is not adding up
articles.summary: US News: 32-year-old Irfan Al-Hussaini died on July 30 in a hospital eight days after he was found unconscious in his Pao Alto apartment which the cops so far .
articles.body: 32-year-old Irfan Al-Hussaini died on July 30 in a hospital eight days after he was found unconscious in his Pao Alto apartment which the cops so far called suicide. Now, his family is seeking a detailed probe, calling the circumstances of the Nvidia scientist's death mysterious. Irfan's parents, sister and attorney held a press conference last week outside Palo Alto City Hall and released new information pertaining to the case. The role of Irfan's wife came on the radar as the family alleged that Irfan was suffering from domestic violence, Kron4, NBC Bay Area reported.Who was Irfan Al-Hussaini?Irfan Al-Hussaini was a Bangladesh-born AI researcher and senior data scientist at NVIDIA. He completed his graduation at Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) in 2017. He moved to the US for higher studies at the Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta. He completed his MS in 2020 and PhD in 2023.Al-Hussaini first interned with NVIDIA from January to May 2022, working on unsupervised learning. After completing his PhD, he joined NVIDIA as a Senior Data Scientist in August 2023.He married Fabia Farlin Athena at Georgia Tech, in Atlanta in 2022.An old social media post of Georgia Tech showed the couple receiving their degrees together. "It took Georgia Tech to bring Irfan Al-Hussaini and Fabia Farlin Athena together. Despite having studied at the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology at the same time, the couple didn’t meet until they came 8,000 miles away to study electrical and computer engineering at Tech. Married in 2022, the two received their doctoral degrees at the Spring 2024 Commencement Ceremony. After that, both will be pursuing careers that reflect their individual and shared dreams — Al-Hussaini at NVIDIA and Athena at Stanford University completing a Stanford Energy Postdoctoral Fellowship," the post said. The post also included their wedding photo.What happened on July 22?According to Irfan's family members, he gave a work presentation around 9am and then sent a Slack message to his manager at 10.02 am that his wife, 'Athi' was not feeling well and that he would have to take the day off for the rest of the day. The family said his colleagues told them that they had no idea about who 'Athi' was.On 10.22 am, someone called 911 and police responded to Irfan's address. Palo Alto police officials allegedly told the family they treated the scene inside his Palo Alto home as a medical emergency, not a suspicious death scene. Irfan was taken to the hospital where he died eight days later.“The adult male was treated by PAFD (Pao Alto Fire Department) on scene and transported to a local hospital where he was later pronounced deceased. At this time, the case is still under investigation pending the report from the medical examiner. We have received materials from the family and others, and our review and investigation is on-going. At this time, neither the police department nor the medical examiner have identified any evidence that the death was the result of foul play," Pao Alto Police Department lieutenant told KRON4.'Impossible for him to take his own life'Irfan's sister Saah Al-Hussaini said her brother had many plans for the future and he was never suicidal. “The circumstances are highly suspicious and raise serious questions about what happened," she said, asking for a clear picture of what happened that day between 10.02 and 10.22 am and whether he sent the message on Slack at all because they said the doctors told them that initial scans suggested Irfan had been without oxygen for nearly 30 to 60 minutes."So who sent that 10:02 text?" Sarah said. "Does that text fit with the medical timeline?"“My brother Irfan was my best friend. It’s impossible to imagine that he took his own life when he was so full of plans for the future. We’ve been left with unanswered questions while the police department and Medical Examiner point fingers at each other," the sister said."The plan that they're supposed to accept is that he hung himself from a door while his wife was home and he did it in a way that she did not detect or know that it was happening," the family's attorney Tony Brass said, as quoted by NBC. "That makes no sense," he said. The family said Irfan was wearing an Oura ring that morning and believes its data could potentially help establish a timeline for investigators.An attorney for Irfan’s widow said she fully cooperated with the investigation and that a full forensic autopsy was performed on August 31. The attorney said Irfan’s widow has no objections to forensic materials being reviewed, the NBC report said.Irfan's friends have started a petition for justice, where they said his marital life was in disarray. "It was widely heard that Athena forced him to cut off all communication with his family and close friends over the past couple of years. Some of his dearest and closest friends, people he has known for almost 2 decades, report that he suddenly stopped all contact with them out of the blue, with no explanation. Many of his peers and his inner social circle, also faced abrupt radio-silence. Such withdrawal was completely out of character for the Irfan everyone knew," the petition said.If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or chat live at 988lifeline.org.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Major US TV networks blackout Trump coverage, protest White House ban on CNN
articles.summary: US News: In a striking move, major US TV networks halt coverage of President Trump after the White House bans CNN, intensifying the conflict between the administration and media outlets. CNN and others file lawsuit claiming violation of First Amendment rights.
articles.body: Major US television networks have suspended their shared television-pool coverage of President Donald Trump after the White House blocked CNN from carrying out its scheduled pool duties, escalating the standoff between the administration and news organisations.Fox News's Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who is acting chair of the television pool consortium, told members that the pool would stop covering presidential events requiring shared access, The Wall Street Journal reported.The pool includes ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC, with the networks taking turns to provide live footage from events where access is limited. The broadcasters also declined to set up an alternative pool for Trump's planned trip to New York for the United Nations General Assembly.The decision followed the White House barring CNN, MS NOW and Politico from its grounds. Trump announced the restrictions on Friday, accusing the outlets of negative coverage and "fake news".The following day, Secret Service agents denied reporters from the three organisations entry to the White House and took their hard-pass press credentials.CNN, MS NOW and Politico responded by filing a federal lawsuit against the Trump administration on Monday. The organisations are also seeking a temporary restraining order, arguing that the restrictions amount to unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination and violate First Amendment protections.In a joint statement, the three organisations said they were suing to "protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes."Trump has defended the restrictions, rejecting claims that his administration is attacking press freedom."The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish," Trump wrote on social media.He had previously defended keeping the outlets out of the White House, saying that if they wanted to publish negative stories, "I don't have to let them into the people's house."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2019, volunteers used 200,000 pounds of discarded oyster shells to build a 400-foot reef protecting a Louisiana tribal shoreline
articles.summary: US News: Along the marshes of southeast Louisiana, the remains of a restaurant meal have found a second life in the water. Oyster shells that might once have b.
articles.body: Along the marshes of southeast Louisiana, the remains of a restaurant meal have found a second life in the water. Oyster shells that might once have been sent to landfill are being collected, cured and returned to the coast, where they can form the base of new reefs. For the Pointe-au-Chien Indian Tribe, the idea took on a more urgent purpose. Erosion had been eating into ancestral land and threatening an earthen mound that held deep cultural significance for the community. As reported by Public Broadcasting Service (PBS), in 2019, hundreds of volunteers helped place about 200,000 pounds of recycled oyster shells along the shoreline, creating a reef about 400 feet long. The structure was intended to slow the loss of land rather than replace it.Louisiana’s coastal erosion put a tribal mound at riskFor Theresa and Donald Dardar, who are leaders of the Pointe-au-Chien Indian Tribe, the changes were visible from a boat travelling through Bayou Pointe-aux-Chenes and the surrounding marshes. Water had been steadily taking pieces of the landscape with it. Among the places at risk were tribal mounds, earthen structures built by Native peoples that serve as important cultural and spiritual sites.One particular mound had become especially vulnerable. It stood roughly 9 to 10 feet above the surrounding marsh, but erosion had removed about four feet of land in front of it over a period of around five years. A large tree remained near the edge, its roots exposed as the shoreline retreated.The tribe generally keeps the locations of its mounds private. In this case, the threat had become difficult to ignore. The Pointe-au-Chien community joined with the Coalition to Restore Coastal Louisiana in 2019 to try to hold the shoreline in place.How restaurant shells became part of the solutionThe material chosen for the project had already served its first purpose. Oyster shells from restaurants in the New Orleans area were being collected instead of discarded and prepared for use in coastal restoration.Volunteers built the first reef for the Pointe-au-Chien Tribe using around 200,000 pounds of shells. The finished structure stretched for about 400 feet along the vulnerable shoreline. A second reef was added later as the work continued.The shells are not simply dropped into the water immediately after collection. They are cleaned and cured for roughly six months before being placed into biodegradable mesh bags. Those bags can then be positioned along the coast, creating a physical foundation on which oysters can settle and grow.Discarded oyster shells helped build a living shoreline in LouisianaOyster reefs have a useful property for coastal restoration: discarded shells provide a surface where young oysters can attach themselves. As oysters grow across the old shells, the reef can become larger and more established. The Coalition to Restore Coastal Louisiana describes these formations as living shorelines because they use natural processes alongside the physical structure to help reduce erosion. The reefs also create habitat. Crabs, fish, shrimp and marine birds can use them, while oysters themselves become part of the developing ecosystem.For the Pointe-au-Chien shoreline, that growth offered something a conventional barrier might not. The aim was not to rebuild the land that had already disappeared, but to give the remaining shoreline some protection from further erosion.Louisiana’s reef grows stronger with oystersThe Dardars later said the living shoreline had withstood strong storms, including Hurricane Ida, which struck Louisiana in 2021. The reef was never presented as a way to restore the lost land. Its purpose was more limited: slow the forces removing what remained. By then, oysters had begun growing large enough to harvest on the first reef. The tribe chose not to collect them, allowing the oyster population to continue developing and adding to the reef instead. That process illustrates why the shells are useful beyond simply being a waste material. Once returned to the water, they can become part of a growing habitat.Louisiana has a huge supply of oyster shellsThe recycling effort is closely tied to the state's seafood industry. Louisiana produces a large share of the oysters consumed in the United States, while millions of oysters harvested in the state are eaten across the country.Once the oysters are shucked, however, the shells are often far from the coast where they could be useful. Disposal can be expensive, particularly when shells are transported from restaurants in cities back towards coastal areas.The Coalition to Restore Coastal Louisiana has spent years developing a system to collect them. By the time of the source report in 2023, its programme had recycled 13 million pounds of oyster shells from New Orleans-area restaurants. As reported by PBS, nearly 50 restaurants were participating.Large bins are collected several times a week, with the shells eventually transported to a stockpile where they can be cured and prepared for restoration projects.Five reefs have protected thousands of feet of coastThe Pointe-au-Chien project was part of a wider programme rather than an isolated experiment. The coalition had completed five reef projects since 2016, with the projects collectively protecting about 8,000 feet of shoreline. Some of the larger installations can extend for almost a mile and use hundreds of tons of recycled shells.The organisation also monitors the reefs as they develop, using satellite and drone imagery to track changes. As cited by PBS, the projects had reduced shoreline erosion by as much as 50%.The figures do not mean every section of Louisiana's disappearing coastline can be protected this way. The projects are relatively small compared with the state's much larger coastal restoration plans. But they provide a way to combine waste collection with habitat creation and shoreline protection.The work extends beyond Pointe-au-ChienThe coalition planned to continue the approach in other Indigenous communities. A future project was scheduled for Grand Bayou Indian Village in Plaquemines Parish, home to the Atakapa-Ishak/Chawasha Tribe and accessible only by water.The need is considerable. Louisiana has more than 800 known mound sites, while ancient earthen mounds along the coast have existed for thousands of years. Anthropologist Jayur Mehta, a co-author of a 2018 study, said the state was losing ancient mounds at a rate of about two a year, taking pieces of the archaeological record with them.For Indigenous communities, the loss is not simply a change in shoreline geography. The mounds are connected to ancestry, community and place.Restaurants became part of the coastal chainThe shell collection programme has also changed how participating restaurants deal with what was once ordinary kitchen waste.Instead of putting shells into rubbish bins, restaurants can separate them for collection. The programme charges participating businesses according to the amount they send for recycling, while scheduled collections remove the material from the restaurants.Louisiana lawmakers also approved a tax incentive for restaurants that recycle oyster shells through qualifying programmes. The measure was expected to reduce the financial burden on participating businesses and encourage wider use of shell recycling.The connection between restaurants and coastal restoration has been taken further through the Chefs on Boats programme. It takes people working in the food industry onto the coast so they can see the journey of an oyster from harvest to restaurant and eventually back into the water as a recycled shell. By the time of the 2023 report, the programme had taken 197 chefs, shuckers, cooks and restaurateurs on 40 trips.For the Pointe-au-Chien Tribe, though, the immediate concern remains much closer to home. The reef cannot reverse every change affecting the Louisiana coast, and the community is also dealing with other damage to the marsh, including canals associated with oil and gas exploration.The oyster shells can only do part of the work. But in a landscape where the shoreline has been steadily disappearing, even a 400-foot stretch of protection has significance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special teaser revealed
articles.summary: Filming wrapped on the BBC Christmas special in October, as fans eagerly await its return.
articles.body:
The first image from The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special has been revealed, teasing a romantic picnic scene.

Inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, the first series was filmed largely in Wales and attracted 7.3 million UK viewers in its first four weeks.

The series finale saw Mary Bennet, played by Ella Bruccoleri, agree to marry Tom Hayward, played by Donal Finn.

Filming wrapped on the BBC three-part Christmas special at the end of October, as fans eagerly await its return.

The first series focused on Mary, the couple's seemingly unremarkable middle daughter as she navigates the societal pressures of Regency England.

It was primarily filmed in south Wales, at locations including Merthyr Mawr in Bridgend county, the Gower peninsula, and Brecon, in Powys.

The Christmas special has been produced by Cardiff-based Bad Wolf, and filming took place over the summer, primarily in Wales.

Gavin & Stacey's Ruth Jones will return to the hit show as Mrs Bennet, who she previously described as "often quite cruel" to her daughter Mary.

Other returning cast members include Ted Lasso's Tanya Reynolds as Caroline Bingley and Laurie Davidson as Mr Ryder.

Also resuming their roles are Varada Sethu as Ann Baxter, Poppy Gilbert as Lizzie Darcy, Maddie Close as Jane Bingley, Grace Hogg-Robinson as Lydia Wickham, Molly Wright as Kitty Buncock and Anna Fenton-Garvey as Charlotte Collins.

Nerys Amber-Stocks, best known for appearing in Out There and Mammoth, joins the cast as Mary's housemaid Lucy.

The show's producer Edoardo Ferretti announced to fans on social media that the special had finished filming at the end of October.

He posted a short but sweet message on Instagram, saying: "And yet another wrap! Every time emotional, every time proud. This one is going to be so special!"

Little has been shared about the plot of the upcoming Christmas special, however, the BBC has teased: "With marriage comes a new identity and the question remains: who will Mary become as Mrs Hayward?"

The three additional episodes, announced in June , will run for 30 minutes each and continue to be based on storylines from the original novel by Janice Hadlow.

It has been written by screenwriter Sarah Quintrell, with Asim Abbasi returning to direct the special.

It will air in the UK on BBC iPlayer and BBC One, while in the US and Canada, it will also be available on BritBox.

Sony Pictures Television will distribute The Other Bennet Sister internationally.

articles.title: In 2019, a Connecticut home renovation uncovered human remains beneath a basement; seven years later, archaeologists found early 'USA' buttons and evidence reshaping the 1777 Battle of Ridgefield
articles.summary: US News: An accidental discovery beneath the floorboards of a Connecticut home during a basement renovation has led to important new findings about the America.
articles.body: An accidental discovery beneath the floorboards of a Connecticut home during a basement renovation has led to important new findings about the American Revolutionary War. In late 2019, contractors working on a 1790 house on Main Street in Ridgefield found human skeletal remains buried in a shallow communal grave. Later investigations by the Connecticut Office of State Archaeology identified the remains as adult men who had been buried without coffins. Physical evidence strongly connected them to the April 1777 Battle of Ridgefield. Years of additional excavation, metal detecting and forensic research, supported by National Park Service grants, have uncovered important military artifacts. These include rare military buttons and lead musket balls that are changing long-held ideas about how the 1777 battle took place.Discovery of early national insigniaAmong the most important finds from recent surveys by the Ridgefield Historical Society and Heritage Consultants, LLC were three pewter military buttons stamped with the initials "USA." Archaeologists say these buttons are the earliest physical evidence found so far of Continental Army enlisted soldiers wearing a common national insignia during the Revolutionary War. Before this discovery, historians generally believed Patriot soldiers in early 1777 were mainly part of separate colonial militias without standard uniforms or national symbols. According to research published by the Ridgefield Historical Society, the "USA" buttons suggest that American troops under Major General David Wooster and Brigadier General Benedict Arnold were already presenting themselves as one army representing a united nation, only ten months after the Declaration of Independence. The buttons were found in the southern part of town, along with dropped "buck and ball" ammunition. This type of ammunition was commonly associated with American forces and combined one large musket ball with several smaller pieces of lead shot.Evidence of a violent British ambushThe archaeological work has also led historians to reconsider the traditional timeline of the battle. The fighting began after about 1,800 British and Loyalist troops under Major General William Tryon raided an American supply depot in Danbury. Patriot forces then attacked the British troops as they retreated toward Long Island Sound. Earlier accounts described the first fighting as small skirmishes as British forces moved toward the main barricade on Main Street. However, the location of recovered musket fire shows that the fighting was much heavier and more chaotic than written records suggested. At the Second Engagement site, researchers found a large concentration of British musket shot along with unused American ammunition. Archaeologists believe British soldiers used the natural cover of a hillside to gather their forces and launch a sudden ambush against Wooster's advancing troops. Artifacts found at the site include a damaged American-made cast musket butt plate, broken French artillery musket fittings and unused lead shot dropped by retreating Continental soldiers. General Wooster was mortally wounded during the surprise attack, which briefly broke up the American lines before the surviving troops regrouped near the center of town.Evidence of an organized retreatEarlier accounts suggested that Patriot troops made a disorganized retreat after British forces broke through the main barricade on Main Street during the Third Engagement. However, evidence from the southern part of town points to a more organized defense. Archaeologists found groups of fired and damaged lead shot from both sides. The pattern suggests that retreating Patriot soldiers repeatedly stopped, took defensive positions and fired directly at advancing British troops. Researchers from the University of Connecticut have also used ground-penetrating radar near the site of the original 2019 discovery. The surveys identified seven additional areas that experts believe could contain more wartime burials. The Connecticut Office of State Archaeology is continuing DNA testing and chemical isotope analysis on the four original skeletons. The research aims to learn more about their geographic origins, diet and possible military connections.Recognition and documentary projectThe research project, involving the Connecticut State Historic Preservation Office, local historians and university researchers, recently received an Award of Merit from Preservation Connecticut for its documentation and community outreach work. The Ridgefield Historical Society is also raising money for a documentary called The Battle of Ridgefield: A New Look at 250. The project is supported in part by a grant from Connecticut Humanities and will document the discoveries and continuing forensic research. The historical society is continuing to catalogue artifacts recovered from all four known engagement areas as researchers prepare for the 250th anniversary of the battle in 2027.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Sawyer Tinsley, a 16-year-old Florida teen who used yard flamingos to raise $25K for rescue pets after fostering a kitten saved her from loneliness
articles.summary: US News: School life is different from what most movies show. While some get to cruise through it in their main character era, others have to suffer through de.
articles.body: School life is different from what most movies show. While some get to cruise through it in their main character era, others have to suffer through deep loneliness where they struggle to find community and support. For Sawyer Tinsley, going to school was overwhelming and lonely. Her first year of middle school was not going well since most of her old friends had shifted to a different school district in Jupiter, Florida. Moreover, due to COVID-19, it was difficult to make new friends with faces behind masks. "You would have to be six feet away, you couldn't really speak, you had masks on, you couldn't really see people. So, it started there when I was just like ... this is hard, like, this is hard to do school in these conditions," she said to WBPF News. "It was the best thing for helping me transition during COVID time when it was really hard."Every day she would rush to her home from school and head straight to her room, sad and frustrated. But one day, when she opened her bedroom door, her mood instantly lifted because waiting there was her latest foster kitten from Palm Beach Purrs. Its loud purring and affectionate nature made her feel less alone and soon she had an idea.Finding love in kittensEver since she was little, Sawyer had wanted a cat. But her family already had three dogs and one of them didn't like cats. When Sawyer was 10, her parents learned about fostering kittens until they were ready for neutering and adoption. “We can give it a try so long as you keep the kitten in your room,” they said.Sawyer loved every one of her foster kittens. Not only did the kitten find a forever home, but she also got another furry feline to help ease her loneliness during a strange school year.One afternoon, something clicked. Sawyer realised that many of her old friends had also expressed their own feelings of isolation. “Hugging a kitten makes me feel so relaxed and less lonely. Maybe it would help my friends, too,” she thought. Thus, to help other middle school girls facing similar challenges, she created a club called 'PAUSE', inviting them to her home to spend time with foster kittens.As soon as some restrictions lifted, Sawyer called a few friends over to play with the kittens. "Would you like to come over and play with a kitten?" she asked and each one of them replied with an enthusiastic yes.As the group of teenagers socialised with the young kittens, they realised that they felt great. “Can we do it again tomorrow?” they asked. Soon, they were bringing more friends and classmates over, eager to make connections."And then they just come and we put them downstairs and then they can just run around. The kids play with them and talk about their, like, stressors (they) have been going through in middle school, cause that's when it starts to like, amp up for elementary school," Sawyer explained.Florida Atlantic University student Chloee Wilkerson, who was taking a break from studying at PetSmart in Palm Beach Gardens, where the foster kittens are located, shared her experience. "It's my favourite coping mechanism. I'll wake up at night to do it, but this is the least consequential one to do," Wilkerson said.Helping the animalsNow 16, Sawyer has fostered nearly 300 kittens. She and her friends, new and old, have come up with a very creative way to raise money for local animal shelters by launching Flamingo Flocking, an annual fundraiser. Every August evening, Sawyer and a few volunteers quietly "flock" a neighbour's yard, planting 15 bright pink plastic flamingos alongside a sign that reads, 'If you donate to help rescue animals, tomorrow you can tell us where to "flock" them next'. Instead of getting annoyed, neighbours have come to love the playful tradition and often eagerly nominate loved ones for a popping pink surprise.Sawyer also sponsors an annual Flamingo 5K run and to date has raised more than $25,000 for local no-kill shelters. “Petting a sweet kitten is so calming,” she said to Woman's World. “If everyone could do it, I think the world would be a thousand times happier.”In the future, she hopes to pursue a career in sports psychology. "Hopefully I am in a successful career and have lots of cats. I gotta have cats and dogs. I love animals," she said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: Two members of a helicopter crew were killed Sunday after their aircraft crashed while taking part in firefighting operations at Yosemite National Park in California, according to the US Forest Service. The identities of the victims have not yet been released.Fly Precision confirms crew members' deathsAerospace company Precision, also known online as Fly Precision, confirmed that two of its crew members died in the crash. The NTSB said its investigators would travel to the site when fire conditions allow and that a preliminary report is expected within 30 days.The Dome Fire, which started on September 15, has continued to spread across Yosemite. articles.title: Five British schoolgirls aged 14 and 15 built a robot with five-metre folding arms designed to create wildfire firebreaks; their two-year-old robotics club is now representing Great Britain globally
articles.summary: UK News: Five schoolgirls from Kent, aged between 14 and 15, have built a robot with five-metre folding arms to help fight wildfires. Their work has earned the.
articles.body: Five schoolgirls from Kent, aged between 14 and 15, have built a robot with five-metre folding arms to help fight wildfires. Their work has earned them the chance to represent Great Britain at an international robotics competition in South Korea. The team from The Folkestone School for Girls, known as Team Meglabyte, designed the robot to clear dry plants and create paths that remove fuel from the spread of fires. The school's robotics club was only founded in 2024, but it has now been chosen to represent Great Britain at the FIRST Global Challenge in Incheon.Designing a solution to growing wildfire risksThe international competition brings together student teams from more than 190 countries to work on major environmental and technology problems. This year's challenge focuses on preventing, controlling and recovering from wildfires in a warming world. For the competition, the Folkestone students designed an autonomous vehicle with long, folding arms that can clear paths up to five metres wide through dry vegetation. The system removes plants and other surface material that can fuel a fire, creating natural firebreaks that can slow the spread of flames without putting firefighters directly in danger. According to a statement on the official website of The Folkestone School for Girls, the students have been working to improve the robot before the global competition: "The Folkestone School for Girls robotics team, Team Meglabyte, are thrilled to be representing Great Britain at the First Global Challenge in South Korea."Working with local firefightersThe five students worked with professional firefighters to make sure their design could deal with the real conditions faced during wildfires. According to a report by Kent news outlet Shepway Vox, the students spoke with Kent Fire and Rescue Service during the early stages of the project. The firefighters helped them understand how wildfires spread across difficult terrain. Their advice led the team to focus on building a lightweight and stable robot that could extend its arms across uneven ground without tipping over. The students also used standard parts supplied by the competition organisers to program the robot's autonomous driving system. The software allows the machine to avoid obstacles, clear debris and work on its own in areas where thick smoke could make remote control difficult.National selection and fundraisingThe team's success comes only two years after the school's robotics program was created. Despite having less experience than some international teams, the Kent students won the national selection process and secured Great Britain's single place in the competition. To help pay for their trip to Incheon and the materials needed to build their robot, the team launched a public crowdfunding campaign. On their official Crowdfunder page, the students explained their goal of representing Britain and encouraging more girls to study science and technology: "Our aim is to inspire young girls across GB into STEM and globally raise awareness about this year's competition theme of wildfires. Each year a single robotics team from a school in Great Britain is sent to compete in a robotics competition on the global stage. This year, five girls from the all-girls state school Folkestone School for Girls have been selected to represent the nation in South Korea to compete with their robot. The girls need your help to get them to the competition!" The students are also using the opportunity to create outreach programs for primary schools. These projects will give younger pupils basic coding kits and lesson plans showing how engineering can be used to solve real environmental problems. The FIRST Global Challenge will take place in Incheon, South Korea, where the five Folkestone students will put their robot to the test against teams from countries around the world.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US Army built an 11-by-8-foot floating island from recycled plastic bottles; native plants now help clean water and shelter wildlife
articles.summary: US News: At a military vehicle wash facility in Texas, an unusual structure is sitting on the surface of a catchment basin. It is only 11 by 8 feet, but its pu.
articles.body: At a military vehicle wash facility in Texas, an unusual structure is sitting on the surface of a catchment basin. It is only 11 by 8 feet, but its purpose extends beyond simply floating. Known as the U.S.S. Eddy, the prototype was built from corrugated pipes packed with recycled plastic bottles, covered with layers of screening and coconut fibre, then planted with native aquatic vegetation. The idea came from staff at Fort Cavazos who were looking for a way to improve water quality while making use of a basin already attracting fish, turtles, frogs, waterfowl and other wildlife. The floating platform was launched in March 2024, as reported by The US Army.How a military wash basin became a testing ground for a floating wetlandThe basin serves a practical military purpose. Tracked vehicles are cleaned with high-pressure water that removes dirt, oil, fluids and other material from their surfaces. Rather than flowing straight away, the wastewater enters the catchment basin, where heavier sediment can settle before the water is recycled for further use.That system leaves the basin holding water containing much finer contaminants as well. The floating island was designed to work within that existing setup rather than replace it.Fort Cavazos' Directorate of Plans, Training, Mobilization and Security, or DPTMS, developed the project with its Adaptive and Integrative Management Team. The intention was to introduce a biological element into the treatment process, using plants and their growing environment as a natural filter.The setting also offered another reason to experiment. Wildlife was already using the area.Inside the unusual design of the U.S.S. EddyThe U.S.S Eddy does not resemble a conventional piece of water-treatment equipment. Its base consists of corrugated pipes filled with discarded plastic bottles. Polyester screen cloth and a coconut liner were added above that framework, creating a surface capable of supporting plants.Native horsetails, pennywort and sedges were selected for the planting layer. Rather than simply placing greenery on a floating platform, the design is intended to create a small living system in which the plants can interact with the water around them.The arrangement gives the island several functions at once. As the vegetation grows, the structure can provide places for wildlife to rest and feed while the plants and their surrounding material contribute to filtration and nutrient cycling.For the people involved in the project, that combination was important. The aim was not just to make the basin's water cleaner. It was also to add habitat to a site that wildlife was already visiting.How the floating island uses plants to filter water naturallyThe floating platform was intended to act in much the same way as a small wetland. Water passes around the plant roots and through the material supporting them, creating opportunities for contaminants and excess nutrients to be captured or processed.The project team said the island was particularly aimed at fine, emulsified contaminants in the basin. It was also expected to help reduce algae and improve the quality of the recycled water through natural processes rather than relying entirely on mechanical treatment.That makes the plants more than decoration. Their roots, growth and interaction with the water are central to how the prototype is supposed to work.There is also a practical wildlife benefit. The basin already supports waterfowl, crawfish, fish, turtles and frogs, while coyotes and raccoons have also been observed around the area. The floating structure gives some of those animals another place to shelter or find food.What happens next for Fort Cavazos' floating island experimentThe March 2024 launch was treated as a trial rather than a finished solution. DPTMS and the AIM Team planned to monitor the island over time, looking at how well the design performed and whether parts of it could be changed.That monitoring could cover everything from the performance of the plants to the durability and efficiency of the floating framework. Lessons from the prototype are intended to guide later versions.The longer-term proposal is considerably larger than the first experiment. Fort Cavazos said it hoped eventually to assemble and launch as many as 20 floating islands.For now, the U.S.S. Eddy remains a relatively small structure on a military catchment basin. Its construction, however, combines several simple elements: waste plastic, recycled water, native plants and a platform designed to support wildlife.The experiment is also taking place in a working facility rather than a purpose-built conservation area. That makes the basin itself part of the test, as the team watches how a floating wetland performs alongside the everyday demands of washing military vehicles.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: He bought three trays of baklava for a concert after a friend bet he couldn't sell them; the business now averages just over $20,000 a month in sales
articles.summary: US News: A New York City baklava seller has turned a small side hustle into a business that now brings in more than $20,000 in monthly sales. Jacob Komarow, kn.
articles.body: A New York City baklava seller has turned a small side hustle into a business that now brings in more than $20,000 in monthly sales. Jacob Komarow, known around the city as the ‘Baklava Guy', started Good Baklava in 2021 after buying three trays of prepared baklava to sell at a Phish concert. A simple bet with a friend soon turned into a growing business. Today, Komarow sells baklava at parks, beaches, festivals, and pop-up events, as well as online. He gets the pastries from a commercial bakery in Turkey. His business gained wider attention after he began selling baklava near Madison Square Garden during the New York Knicks’ championship run.How the Baklava Guy turned a concert bet into a $20,000-a-month businessKomarow’s business started with a simple experiment in September 2021. While travelling to a Phish concert in California, he bought three trays of pre-made baklava from a Middle Eastern grocery store and challenged a friend to see if he could sell them. He managed to sell all three trays and tripled his money. At the time, Komarow was six months sober and had recently lost his first full-time marketing job, so he relied on freelance work and baklava sales to cover his expenses.For nearly three years, he continued selling baklava at Phish concerts before taking the business to other outdoor events. A major shift came in spring 2022, when he tried a pistachio-heavy Turkish baklava from a vendor in Paterson, New Jersey. The experience eventually led him to the supplier in Turkey that now provides his baklava.How Good Baklava’s Madison Square Garden sales became a turning pointGood Baklava’s recent growth accelerated after Komarow began selling outside Madison Square Garden during the Knicks’ championship run. He handed out free slices, filmed the appearances and shared the videos online, helping the business attract a much larger audience. A New York Times profile brought another wave of attention, which Komarow described as a ‘baklava wildfire’. He said the company’s Instagram audience grew by 20% overnight after the story was published, while brands began reaching out about partnerships.Good Baklava has since worked with companies and restaurants, creating new business opportunities. As per CNBC, the business recorded slightly more than $20,000 in monthly sales over a recent nine-month period. The figure covers street sales, pop-ups, wholesale orders and online purchases.Why the business still faces unpredictable months despite strong salesThe recent attention has brought strong sales for Good Baklava, but the business has also experienced sharp swings from one month to the next. Its strongest month came in December 2025, when sales approached $70,000, helped by holiday orders and customer traffic at New York’s Union Square Holiday Market. Sales fell below $10,000 the following month, highlighting how much the business can depend on seasons, events, and temporary locations.Alongside these fluctuations, Komarow has ongoing costs for shipping, packaging, marketing, and Shopify fees. The company also has about 11 part-time workers who handle marketing, administration, packing and pop-up operations. Temporary markets can bring additional permit and insurance expenses. When selling from parks or his van, Komarow says he sometimes faces police intervention over permits, although he has not been arrested or fined.How Komarow’s street sales strategy keeps changing with every customerFor Komarow, selling baklava is as much about conversation as it is about the pastry itself. Whether he is in Prospect Park, Rockaway Beach, or at a concert, he approaches people with a tray and asks if they would like to buy some baklava. He compares the approach to stand-up comedy, saying each interaction helps him understand what works. His pitch can move from small talk and jokes to explaining his Turkish baklava and the ‘Good Baklava; No Drugs’ shirts he wears.Once customers show interest, he explains the pastry, where it comes from, and how much it costs. Three pieces usually sell for $10, while seven cost $20. At some music festivals, three pieces can cost $15. Years of testing different introductions, phrases, and approaches have helped Komarow refine his sales pitch in real time.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
